name: The Real-Life Money Manual
place: Welcome to your financial home base
strap: Some assembly required. You’ve got this.
description: Give everyday bills, safety nets, debt, and long-term plans a place to live.
tone: The appliance warranty is not a personality test.

topics.title: Build from the money that actually lands.
topics.text: A salary comes with a headline number and a number your bank account actually meets. Gross pay is earnings before taxes and other deductions. Take-home pay is what reaches you. Build the spending plan from that second number, covering regular needs, debt payments, and occasional bills. Net worth is another useful number: assets minus debts. Each number tells a different part of the story.
topics.aside: Our fictional household takes home $2,800 a month and uses $2,200 for essentials and required payments. These invented amounts show a relationship, not what your salary should be.
topics.joke: The salary sounded bigger before it met the deductions.
topics.prompt: Toggle between the whole amount and the essentials.
topics.term: CASH FLOW IS A FLOW; NET WORTH IS A SNAPSHOT
topics.everyday: A new job may introduce you to benefit documents, commuting costs, rent, taxes, and a surprisingly sociable collection of bills. Read the pay statement and benefit terms so the plan reflects what you receive and what you owe. Set aside money for less frequent costs, too. You can own valuable things and still be short of spendable cash next week. Check the balance sheet and the calendar.
topics.connection: Start the spending plan with the money that arrives after deductions. Give that money jobs before the bills assign their own.
words: Gross pay
Pay before taxes and other deductions take their share.
Take-home pay
The cash pay that remains after deductions.
Net worth
What you own minus what you owe, measured at a particular time.
topics.assumptions: All money amounts and timing are invented for teaching. This is not a survey of prices, income, or tax rates. The flow view is a single example, not a recommended allocation.

topics.title: Your priorities need calendar space.
topics.text: A useful budget has room for obligations, flexible spending, and things you are working toward. Percentage rules can offer a starting sketch, but your rent and responsibilities may have strong opinions about it. If essentials exceed income, the gap needs practical attention. Revisit the plan when work, household needs, or responsibilities change. Your budget is allowed to keep up with your life.
topics.aside: After essentials, this example leaves $600. Split it between flexible spending and a $1,200 goal. Different splits produce different timelines; there is no official perfect split hiding in the slider.
topics.joke: A spreadsheet cannot negotiate your rent. Annoyingly.
topics.prompt: Change flexible spending and observe what happens to the goal.
topics.term: PLAN FOR YOUR LIFE, NOT SOMEONE ELSE’S RATIO
topics.everyday: Start by separating commitments from expenses you can change quickly. Include goals and irregular bills. If you share a household, talk about who pays what before the next bill becomes a small domestic mystery. Automatic payments and transfers can help, provided the cash is there on time. When housing or care costs overwhelm income, a few skipped treats may barely touch the gap. Look at the larger costs and available support.
topics.connection: Build a plan for your priorities and your actual circumstances. That is the life the money has to support.
words: Budget
A plan for using income to cover obligations, spending, and saving.
Opportunity cost
The next-best use of the money you give up when you choose.
Reserve
Money given a future job and set aside until it is needed.
topics.assumptions: Essentials are fixed in this illustration. Flexible spending and saving divide the remaining money. Goal periods = ceiling(goal ÷ saving per period). No interest, price changes, or income changes are modeled.

topics.title: Resilience has more than one tool.
topics.text: A financial cushion gives an unexpected bill somewhere to land. How much cash to keep ready depends on your obligations, risks, and support. Insurance can cover specified losses in exchange for a premium, with limits, deductibles, and exclusions. Saving, insurance, and reducing expensive debt each help in different ways. Your plan needs a few tools in the drawer.
topics.aside: Start with $100, add savings for six months, and reveal a $450 repair. This illustration shows what a cash cushion can do; your full plan also has other needs to balance.
topics.joke: An emergency fund can change surprises from catastrophic to just annoying.
topics.prompt: Explore a saving pace, then see what the repair uses.
topics.term: RESILIENCE = ACCESSIBLE CASH + A PLAN FOR RISKS
topics.everyday: An annual insurance bill is expected, even if it always seems to arrive with theatrical timing. Plan for it. A surprise repair may use emergency savings. Your income stability, dependents, and access to help can affect how large a reserve makes sense. Keep up with required debt payments while building it, and check what your insurance actually covers. Cash and coverage work together, but they do different jobs.
topics.connection: A cushion helps keep a surprise cost from rearranging your whole budget without asking.
words: Emergency fund
Savings you can reach when an unplanned cost or loss of income arrives.
Premium
The amount you pay for insurance coverage.
Deductible
An amount you may need to pay before particular coverage pays.
Exclusion
A loss or situation the insurance policy leaves out.
topics.assumptions: Savings = starting cash + contribution × periods. A surprise is subtracted once when switched on. Savings cannot go below zero; the remaining cost is shown separately. No interest, investment returns, insurance payment, or new borrowing is included.

topics.title: Debt has a price and a schedule.
topics.text: Borrowing has a price tag and a calendar. Interest is part of that price, and fees may add more. Extra payments on high-interest debt can reduce later interest, but using every available dollar could leave you short when a need turns up. Cover required payments, compare the terms, and keep essential cash in view. The goal is a plan you can sustain.
topics.aside: Try payments on a fictional $1,500 card balance at 24% APR. There are no fees or new charges in the model, and your other bills are outside this illustration.
topics.joke: Your credit card would love to be in a long-term relationship.
topics.prompt: Compare payment amounts, payoff time, and interest cost.
topics.term: COST, LIQUIDITY, AND OBLIGATIONS BELONG IN THE SAME PLAN
topics.everyday: A high interest rate deserves attention, along with rent and the rest of your obligations. Check for variable rates, penalties, or benefits that could affect the comparison. Start with the payments you must make, then consider what extra repayment fits. If the debt has become hard to manage, the lender or a reputable nonprofit credit counselor may be able to explain options. You do not need to solve the whole tangle alone.
topics.connection: Paying extra can cut future borrowing costs. Keeping accessible savings can help you handle a change of plans. Consider both jobs.
words: Principal
The amount borrowed that remains to be paid back, separate from interest.
APR
An annual percentage rate used to describe borrowing cost.
Interest
What you pay for using borrowed money.
Liquidity
Having money available when an obligation comes due.
topics.assumptions: Interest = opening balance × APR ÷ 12, then the fixed payment is applied. The last payment may be smaller. No new charges, fees, daily calculation, payment timing variation, or tax effects. The comparison payment is a fictional fixed amount, not a real issuer’s minimum-payment schedule.

topics.title: Let the long term be long term.
topics.text: Compounding gives earlier growth a chance to earn more growth. Investments can also fall, so match their risk to when you need the money and what losses you can handle. Diversification reduces concentration risk, fees take a share, and inflation changes buying power. If you have an employer plan, read the matching and vesting rules. The useful details tend to live beyond the cheerful brochure cover.
topics.aside: Watch a fictional $1,000 grow at 5% a year, with 2% inflation. The buying-power figure is before tax. Real returns fluctuate, however politely the line behaves here.
topics.joke: Retirement You has requested a seat at the budget meeting.
topics.prompt: Change the years. Compare account dollars and buying power.
topics.term: ACCOUNT DOLLARS AND BUYING POWER ARE DIFFERENT
topics.everyday: An employer match can be valuable, but the formula and vesting rules tell you what is available and when it becomes yours. Accounts also differ in tax treatment and withdrawal limits. Compare diversification and ongoing costs alongside performance. Be wary of promises of high returns with no risk. Money for an approaching move or emergency has a deadline; it should not need the market to be in a cooperative mood.
topics.connection: Your long-term plan starts with the everyday plan: cash flow, a cushion, borrowing costs, and money you can leave working for longer.
words: Compounding
Growth earning further growth over time.
Purchasing power
What a sum of money can actually buy.
Vesting
The rules saying when certain employer contributions become yours.
Diversification
Spreading investments to reduce concentration risk; market losses are still possible.
topics.assumptions: Nominal ending value = principal × (1 + (gross return − annual fee)/100)^years. Purchasing power divides that value by (1 + inflation/100)^years. Subtracting the fee from annual return is a simplified convention. The optional 20% drop is applied once at the end, to both comparison paths. No taxes, contributions, or changing returns. These are scenarios, not promised outcomes.

recap: Plan with take-home pay and irregular bills.
Adjust the budget to your circumstances.
Understand compounding, inflation, fees, and risk.
action: Review one bill, due date, or benefit.
Read a plan’s fees and matching terms.
artAlt: An apartment with a couch, a plant, a checklist, and a key.

review.title: The real-life readiness check
review.intro: Five questions. No one will ask you to assemble a bookshelf afterward. Probably.
summary: Track income, bills, and dates together so the money is there when needed.
Give essentials, flexible spending, and future goals realistic jobs in your budget.
An accessible reserve and insurance can address different parts of a surprise; coverage has conditions.
A loan creates future payments. Compare total cost and affordability, not just the monthly number.
Investing choices depend on goals, time, fees, and risk. Hypothetical growth is not a promised outcome.

questions.prompt: Why track bill dates as well as monthly totals?
choices: Money must be available when a payment is due
questions.explanation: A positive monthly total can still hide a shortfall mid-month. Your budget needs both an amount and a calendar; the calendar has a surprisingly active role.

questions.prompt: What is the opportunity cost of using money for one goal?
choices: The alternative use you give up
A fee charged on every purchase
Proof the goal is a bad choice
questions.explanation: Choosing one use limits what that money can do elsewhere. A tradeoff is not a moral verdict; it helps you decide which job matters most right now.

questions.prompt: Why might savings still matter if you have insurance?
choices: Deductibles, exclusions, or timing can leave costs to cover
questions.explanation: A policy covers particular risks under particular terms. Accessible savings can cover a deductible or a gap. Read the conditions; the policy title is not the entire plot.

questions.prompt: Which comparison gives a fuller picture of two borrowing offers?
choices: Rate, fees, term, total repayment, and fit with future cash flow
questions.explanation: A smaller monthly payment can spread costs over longer and increase total interest. Compare the full agreement and what future budgets can support. Slogans rarely make payments.

questions.prompt: Which statement about investing and time is sound?
choices: A longer horizon guarantees a profit
Time affects compounding, but losses remain possible
questions.explanation: Compounding works over time, and fees affect what stays invested. Risk still matters. A future goal deserves assumptions you understand, rather than a chart auditioning as a crystal ball.
